# Discussion

This thesis set out to adapt a connectivity modeling framework for wild boar by building an empirically calibrated resistance surface, to develop an interactive QGIS plugin for testing landscape modifications, and to produce scenario-contrast visualisations for wildlife authorities in Canton Zürich. The following sections evaluate how far each objective was reached, place the findings in context, and set out the principal uncertainties.

## Ecological Interpretation of the iSSF Model

All seven retained covariates were positive predictors of transit movement, confirming that wild boar in directed movement prefer denser forest at both scales and greater distance from every class of transport and settlement infrastructure. This matches the established ecology of the species, which depends on continuous forest cover for movement and strongly avoids traffic, light, and disturbance [@morelle2015; @guberti2019]. Two features of the coefficient structure stand out. Forest density at the 50-metre scale carried by far the smallest standard error, reflecting the central role of immediate cover. Distance to railway carried a nearly identical point estimate but with a much larger standard error, most likely because railways are sparse in the Aargau training area and few transit steps were recorded near them, so the avoidance effect is real but its magnitude is less certain. The positive coefficients at both forest scales indicate selection for cells that are both locally wooded and embedded in a forested matrix, consistent with hierarchical habitat selection [@avgar2016]. The non-significance of slope and terrain ruggedness reflects the modest relief of the lowland training area and should not be generalised, since terrain may well enter a model calibrated in more rugged landscapes.

The exclusion of distance to fenced roads is a transferable methodological point. Including it produced an ecologically implausible apparent attraction toward motorway fencing, an artifact of animals pacing along impassable barriers and generating dense telemetry clusters. Handling such hard barriers through the deterministic burn-in rather than as a step-selection covariate is the correct response, and any iSSF study in a landscape with dense linear barriers should apply the same check before finalising variable selection.

## Resistance Surface Quality and Transfer Validity

The Aargau surface reproduces the expected corridor structure, with low resistance along the forested Jura slopes and the Aare and Reuss riparian forests and high resistance across the agricultural plain and peri-urban areas. The median resistance well above the scale midpoint confirms that the lowland landscape is predominantly unfavourable for transit, consistent with its known fragmentation [@fischer2024]. Assigning dense settlement the maximum resistance rather than NoData is a deliberate compromise: wild boar do enter urban fringes nocturnally [@guberti2019; @morelle2015], so treating settlement as an absolute barrier would suppress pathways that occur in reality, and pathways routed through such cells should be read as rare but possible.

Transferring the Aargau parameters to Zürich is operationally necessary because no Zürich telemetry was available, and it rests on the assumption that wild boar respond to forest and infrastructure similarly in both cantons. This is plausible given their shared Mittelland structure and the broadly consistent habitat preferences of European wild boar [@morelle2015], but the more intensively urbanised Greater Zürich landscape may host animals with modified avoidance responses that the Aargau coefficients do not capture. Reusing the Aargau scaling parameters is what keeps the coefficients interpretable, while the Zürich-specific final normalisation maximises corridor contrast within Zürich at the cost of cross-cantonal comparability, an acceptable trade-off for a tool strictly focused on intra-cantonal spatial planning. The pipeline is structurally designed to ingest new infrastructure layers dynamically. This modularity transforms the resistance surface from a static map into an interactive epidemiological planning tool, enabling authorities to simulate the spatial containment effects of proposed barrier networks on wild boar movement. Ultimately, this ecologically calibrated resistance landscape provides the robust foundation necessary for simulating the functional ecological network using connectivity algorithms.

## The Planning Tool in Context

The central advance over the static models of @fischer2024 and @urbina2023 is interactivity. Both provide rigorous maps of the current landscape but cannot answer the what-if questions that ASF management requires. The plugin closes this gap: a user can draw a fence across a pinchpoint, re-run the model, and see directly how the corridor backbone, the infection-risk zones, and the contamination surface respond. This addresses the trade-off @hess1994 identified, where the same corridor that benefits a species can accelerate disease, by showing both sides of a specific intervention rather than a general map.

The five modules are complementary rather than redundant. Least-cost paths give the optimal routes, circuit theory reveals bottlenecks and redundancy that a single path cannot [@mcrae2008], the infection-risk raster expresses cost-distance as an EFSA-anchored probability that veterinary authorities can read directly, the biased correlated random walk offers an independent stochastic check that converges toward the circuit result [@saerens2009], and the individual-based model adds an epidemiological layer by simulating disease trajectories conditioned on an ASF infectious period. Using the published Circuitscape.jl solver, with settings matching @urbina2023, favours a validated implementation over a custom one, while the scipy fallback preserves the capability where Julia is unavailable.

## Limitations and Sources of Uncertainty

The most significant limitation is the absence of formal validation. The iSSF fit was not quantified with concordance statistics or spatial cross-validation, and predictive performance on held-out Aargau steps was not assessed, so the relationship between modeled resistance and actual movement probability remains uncertain [@avgar2016]. The Zürich surface is entirely unvalidated, since no Zürich tracks were available to test the transferred corridors, which adds a layer of uncertainty to management decisions based on the Zürich map. A gap of roughly ten years separates the 2014 to 2017 telemetry from the 2026 landscape data, so infrastructure and land cover changes are not reflected in the behavioural calibration, and their net effect was not assessed. The 15-minute fix interval reliably captures directed transit [@podgorski2013; @benhamou2014] but the conservative classifier may exclude some shorter in-matrix steps, slightly underestimating selection strength, though the large retained sample and high significance of all predictors suggest the coefficients are robust. Finally, the plugin modules carry their own assumptions: the infectious-period distribution is calibrated to Eastern European and Baltic populations [@efsa2018; @probst2017; @chenais2019] whose disease course may differ from ASF-naive Swiss wild boar, and the static movement kernel does not capture nocturnal or seasonal variation in space use.

## Practical Implications and Outlook

The tool is primarily a pre-outbreak planning instrument. Its main value is enabling authorities to identify high-risk corridors and prioritise fence locations before an incursion, with the pinchpoint map showing where a small barrier achieves the greatest reduction in connectivity and the infection-risk raster showing which zones would require surveillance under EFSA guidelines. The scenario comparison supports the iterative decision-making that operational management needs, letting an officer test alternative fence alignments in a single session without programming or reprocessing.

The pipeline follows the FAIR principles of the ZHAW reproducibility requirement, drawing on publicly accessible federal geodata except for the partner-provided telemetry and fence data, with the full workflow encoded in documented notebooks and the plugin distributed as an installable QGIS package reusable in other cantons. Three extensions would add the most value. The highest priority is obtaining GPS telemetry from Zürich wild boar to validate the transferred surface against independent movement data. A seasonal decomposition of the iSSF would reflect the substantial behavioural shifts between winter mast foraging and the active season [@morelle2015]. Finally, weighting the outputs by estimated wild boar density would add the host-abundance dimension that, together with connectivity, drives epidemic spread [@guberti2019].
